Beyond household services

Shared expertise

Research enters through a field where customer work and research require the same assessed qualification.

Following the household’s tax return has shown how a technology developed elsewhere reaches a profession through its customers, changing purchased work, retained experience, and the return to qualification inside that occupation. We now extend the service economy to a field whose assessed expertise is also used in research, so the people qualified to perform customer work can divide their time between serving customers and producing new knowledge.

Within this extension, the same portable qualification supports both activities, and the shared wage carries changes in customer demand into the cost of research. Our career mechanism continues to determine how many qualified people become available, while completed research advances the frontier supplying future customer capability, closing a connection between occupational adjustment and technological progress.

To give research demand an explicit source, we assign a fund a fixed expenditure flow and a mandate to purchase completed, validated research packets, whose cost includes generation and checking. Within the human method, both stages use expert time together with computation, while a feasible autonomous method purchases both stages through computation, allowing procurement to compare two complete ways of producing a result.

Because each packet includes every stage required for completion, validation can determine the eventual productivity of the method even as generation becomes faster. We first follow the hours and computation needed to finish that work, then allow their market prices to determine which method the fund purchases and how its decision affects the earnings available to qualified people.

Research methods

Equal packet costs

Inside a mixed allocation, additional expertise changes method shares while output per unit of budget stays fixed.

At the wage that clears customer services alone, every expert works on customer files, while a fund purchasing human research adds another claim on those hours and raises the clearing wage. Comparing these two wages with the wage at which human and machine packets have equal costs determines whether research employs people, computation, or a mixture of both.

When human research remains cheaper even at the higher clearing wage, the fund spends its budget on human packets and employs the hours that its wage-plus-compute expense permits. When the autonomous route is cheaper at the service-only wage, the fund purchases machine packets and the professional wage clears customer work alone.

Between those cases, equal packet costs fix the wage while labor clearing determines how much human research fits beside customer services, and the remaining budget purchases autonomous packets. Extra expertise then increases the human share at that fixed wage, with each dollar still purchasing the same quantity of completed research, giving a local regime where frontier output is independent of expert headcount.

Holding the frontier fixed lets us follow how inherited expertise and customer demand divide today’s research budget, because each method then has a given generation and validation requirement. Along a career path, those inherited quantities change as people learn and research advances, so dynamic equilibrium carries the same clearing conditions from one date to the next.

Preparing the figure

Hours and entrants

At a human research allocation, customer preparation that saves expert time releases hours from professional work and reduces the wage needed to clear the shared market, allowing the fixed research fund to purchase more labor. Because services also expand when the wage falls, research receives a fraction of the released time, with that fraction determined by the responsiveness of both service demand and research demand.

Along a career transition, the same preparation can reduce diagnostic entry and leave fewer qualified people available later, raising the wage paid by the fund at a common frontier. Both channels appear in the local research formula, where the change in expert population enters with the opposite sign to the change in service demand measured at the old wage.

For an exact finite comparison after customer task requirements settle, eventual human research rises when the professional hours released at the old wage exceed the loss of expert supply evaluated at the old training incentive. Holding service demand fixed gives lower eventual research labor after practice loss, while sufficiently large service savings reverse that ordering, a threshold proved on pages 48–49.

When a machine method requires a residual human grounding stage, each completed machine packet again purchases some expert time, so expertise changes its cost and research output at the grounded corner. Full autonomous validation and human grounding consequently imply different local responses, with equal-cost mixing still able to absorb changes through method shares.

Future research earnings

Within an interior mixed allocation, the equal-cost wage follows the relative productivities of the two complete research methods, and a faster-improving machine route can lower that wage as the frontier advances. Announced reductions in future machine requirements then change the earnings available over a novice’s career, so their effect on training begins when the announcement changes expectations.

In the paper’s joint comparison, both economies remain mixed, share the same initial states and terminal qualification payoff, and face identical methods until the adoption date. When the improved machine route has productivity elasticity at least as large as the human route over the relevant interval, adoption produces a weakly faster frontier and a weakly lower wage path, which lowers current qualification value and study whenever future wages fall strictly over a positive interval.

Because the frontier and wage paths agree before adoption within that comparison, the reduction in initial training comes through expected future returns, while current research allocation remains governed by today’s costs. Proposition H.4 gives the argument, and the welfare chapter follows the further question of how the value received by an individual worker relates to the value of the research that worker supports.
